prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a simple, general mechanism that I find convincing: at the magic wavelength the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated simultaneously. This reduces quantum projection noise and removes Doppler and recoil shifts at once. The idea can be stated cleanly, it was realised experimentally, and it has been reproduced at the 1e-18 level by several independent laboratories. The two-name attribution is compact (Katori for the proposal and first demonstration, Ye for the record accuracy and the many-body clock physics). The candidate drew the broadest support in the opening ballots, with five top-three rankings. Having reread the opening ballots, I find that this support rests on independent scientific arguments about originality, reproducibility and attribution, not on a shared impression. That persuades me more than my own first choice has persuaded anyone else.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a precision-measurement invention in a field that already has two prizes in nearby territory (frequency combs in 2005, ion control in 2012). A committee could regard it as an incremental refinement of the optical clock programme rather than a new discovery. Several members note that the formal redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened, so the full impact is still prospective. There is also a smaller attribution risk: Lemonde, Ludlow and others contributed, and the credit of the trapped-ion clock groups is not settled in the supplied material. My own first-ranked candidate, conformal field theory (B001), has a more general conceptual reach, but its credited names omit Belavin and it has no support from colleagues, so I cannot honestly claim a committee case for it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique opening new observations (geodesy, fundamental constants, dark matter), with a clean two-laureate allocation, and notes that the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I agree on the allocation and on the reproducibility, and I would not make the prize wait for the redefinition: the scientific claim, uncertainty near 1e-18 confirmed across independent labs, is already established. Where I qualify his view is the word 'decisive'. The geodesy and dark-matter applications are promising but still mostly projected, so the citation should rest on the invention and realisation and should not promise those uses.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a genuine conceptual step and not an incremental improvement, because magic-wavelength trapping gives many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime with controlled quantum projection noise and Doppler/recoil shifts, and she doubts whether the committee will see it as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: Her mechanistic argument is the one that moves me, since it identifies a single idea that explains why the clock works. On distinctness I would push further than she does: the 2005 prize covered the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize covered control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock achieves its stability by interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms with systematic shifts cancelled by design. I think the committee can defend that difference in the citation, but I accept that the judgement is not free of doubt.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B016) first and DMFT (B018) second, valuing a new class of states defined by topology and a controlled framework for strongly correlated electrons.
responses.response: I ranked both of these highly and respect the argument, but I would qualify it on B016. As Eriksson himself notes, the credit for the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and for the 3D case lies outside the supplied names, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves out decisive contributors, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. For B018 the Metzner credit for the infinite-dimension limit is similarly missing, and DMFT is closer to a method than a discovery. I therefore do not think either is a cleaner attribution case than the lattice clock, although I would keep B017 in view as a better-defined theory-plus-experiment pair.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B009) first as the architecture behind superconducting processors and the natural continuation of the 2025 prize, and discloses his proximity to the field through WACQT and Chalmers.
responses.response: I thank him for the disclosure, which is the right way to handle it. My disagreement is about timing: B009 follows so soon after the 2025 award on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits that the committee would have to argue the distinction between strong light-matter coupling on a chip and that earlier result, and Kroll raises the same doubt independently. He also concedes that the three-name cut (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) leaves out Girvin and others. That argues for waiting a few years on B009, not for dismissing it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics (B042) first as a tool that opened routine sub-angstrom imaging, and she asks colleagues to test whether her judgement is balanced or parochial.
responses.response: Her request for a check is fair, and my own check is that the credited names are a coherent set but incomplete: Krivanek, who did the corrected STEM work, is not among them, and the microscopy lineage already holds Ruska in 1986. I also see an open question about whether this belongs in physics or in chemistry, where cryo-EM was honoured in 2017. Taken together these are why I rank it below the lattice clock, although I do not dispute its impact on materials physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether to credit Lemonde, Ludlow or other early contributors, and whether the two-name allocation survives a check of priority dates; I have not verified exact priority dates myself.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second.
Whether a theoretical-physics prize such as conformal field theory (B001) could attract any support given the missing Belavin credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B014. I note, as a general matter, that I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), and that he has flagged his proximity to circuit QED and she to electron microscopy; I have no collaboration with the candidates in B014, B001, B017 or B016.
